chunks: "In a regulator, the load line, or droop, means the DC output voltage is intentionally made to drop as the load current increases: V out equals V ref-R LL times I out .
R LL is a virtual output resistance of a milliohm or two. You do it by sensing the load current and subtracting a proportional term from the voltage the controller regulates to.
Why would you want worse regulation? Because of transients.
A processor rail has a tolerance window, say plus or minus 30 millivolts around 1 volts, and a load step of tens of amps.
Without droop, I sit in the middle of the window and can only use half of it for undershoot when the load steps up. With droop, I sit at the top of the window at no load.
When the load steps up, the output falls toward the bottom, and if R LL matches the output impedance of the converter, it falls exactly along the load line, using the whole window.
So the output capacitance I need roughly halves, overshoot at unload is smaller, and the load runs at a lower voltage when it's busy, which saves dynamic power since it goes with V squared .
The trade-offs are that DC accuracy gets worse, because the voltage at full load is a deliberate 60 millivolts or so lower.
The load has to work at the low end of the window at maximum current.
I also need accurate current sensing, including temperature drift of an inductor-DCR sensor, and I have to tune the loop so that the droop matches the real output impedance."
